desc:
An apple tree bears fruit for n days. On day i (counting from 0) it grows apples[i] new apples, and these apples rot after days[i] days, which means they can be eaten on days i, i+1, ..., i + days[i] - 1 and not later. A day with apples[i] = 0 grows nothing.

You eat at most one apple per day, and you may keep eating after day n - 1 as long as unrotten apples remain. Return the maximum number of apples you can eat.

apples = [1, 2, 3, 5, 2], days = [3, 2, 1, 4, 2]
result = 7
batches: {1 apple, days 0-2}, {2 apples, days 1-2}, {3 apples, day 2 only}, {5 apples, days 3-6}, {2 apples, days 4-5}
day 0: batch 0   day 1: batch 1   day 2: batch 1 (batch 2 would rot next day, but one apple per day only)
day 3: batch 3   day 4: batch 4   day 5: batch 4   day 6: batch 3   -> 7 apples
hints: Each day you have to decide which batch to eat from. Think of each batch as having a deadline.
Eating the apples that rot soonest first never hurts: apples that expire later can still be eaten on the following days.
Keep a min-heap of batches keyed by their last edible day. Each day add today's batch, drop batches that already rotted, and eat one apple from the batch on top.
editorial: This is a scheduling problem with unit tasks and deadlines: every apple is a task that must be done by the last edible day of its batch, and each day offers one slot. Earliest-deadline-first is optimal: if an optimal plan eats a later-expiring apple on a day when an earlier-expiring one was available, swapping them keeps every apple edible and the count unchanged.

Simulate day by day. Maintain a min-heap of [last edible day (exclusive), remaining count]. On day i, push today's batch if it has apples, pop batches whose expiry is at most i, then decrement the count of the top batch and add one to the answer; remove the batch from the heap when its count reaches 0. Continue past day n - 1 until the heap is empty.
The loop runs at most n + max(days) iterations (at most 23,000 here), each with O(log n) heap work. Memory is O(n).
